details.text: Severe clusters of strong to occasionally severe storms may gradually move into a more unstable air mass this evening. Some potential for MCS development and a subsequent severe wind gust risk is evident. Confidence is low, but a Watch is possible

details.label: Discussion
details.text: As of 0100 UTC, regional radar imagery showed several clusters of strong to occasional severe storms ongoing from southern WY, across eastern CO into southwestern KS. Driven in part by a broad post-frontal upslope flow regime, convective coverage has steadily increased this evening. With numerous storms ongoing, some cold pool amalgamation has been noted. Recent CAM guidance shows this continuing with a potentially more organized cluster or MCS evolving later this evening. The air mass to the north of the front is still relatively warm and moist which is supporting moderate buoyancy (MLCAPE 1500-2500 J/kg). Deep-layer shear is more modest between 25-35 kt, but slightly elongated mid and upper-level hodographs are supportive of some organization of multicells and clusters. Overall shear profiles are also expected to increase later this evening with the nocturnal low-level jet. The primary uncertainty remains the storm-scale organization of the cold pool and how that may influence the severe risk. With the environment more than supportive of strong updrafts and current storm maintenance, further clustering and eventual organization is possible, especially where low-level convergence is maximized along and north of the front. Given this potential, some severe risk could evolve later this evening and overnight. The need for a watch is very uncertain, but conditions will be monitored

details.label: Most probable threats
details.text: MOST PROBABLE PEAK WIND GUST...65-80 MPH · MOST PROBABLE PEAK HAIL SIZE...UP TO 1.25 IN

details.label: Summary
details.text: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms ongoing over parts of the eastern Great Basin and Intermountain West may pose a risk for isolated strong/severe gusts this evening. Storm organization will be limited and a watch is unlikely

details.label: Discussion
details.text: As of 2310 UTC, regional radar and visible imagery showed numerous thunderstorms ongoing within a plume of monsoon moisture over the eastern Great Basin. Over the last hour, a more robust cluster of storms has emerged across parts of northwestern UT. The environment downstream remains warm and quite moist, with dewpoints in the low 50s F. This is supporting around 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE across northern and central UT, which will be sufficient for strong updrafts. While the air mass is more moist than typical with PWATS near or exceeding 1 inch, area RAP soundings show steep lapse rates in the lowest 1-2 km with T/TD spread around 30 degrees F. This is more than sufficient to support stronger downdrafts and strong/severe gusts within the ongoing convection, especially with the more clustered storms. Some hail will also be possible with the stronger intermittent cores. Several mesonet sites have already reported gusts in the 45-50 kt range. This looks likely to continue as convective coverage slowly increases. While strong/severe gusts will be possible into this evening, little in the way of storm organization is expected owing modest deep-layer shear around 20 kt. This suggest the strongest storms are likely to be transient. Additionally, convection will gradually move eastward into a cooler air mass with weaker lapse rates and buoyancy across northern UT and far southwest WY this evening. This suggests the overall risk for severe gusts and hail should be isolated and a Watch is unlikely
